solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Plates and saucers etc, still not drinking cups!

indicators.note: to cup something is to hold it in curved hands, so one piece wraps around another

parts.note: TT is short for teetotal, someone who does not drink alcohol
as verbs, to still and to ease both mean to calm

explanation.surface: A sober host proudly shows off a crockery collection, pointedly not drinking from any of the cups.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' looks like the adverb meaning yet, but here it is the verb meaning calm. TT for teetotal sits either side of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A matching collection of cups, saucers, plates and pot used for serving tea is exactly what that phrase names.

clue.text: Name coming up in Waugh, in impartial manner

indicators.note: the abbreviation for name moves higher up this down entry, which rearranges the letters

parts.note: Evelyn Waugh was an English novelist, author of Brideshead Revisited

explanation.surface: A critic hopes a name mentioned in a Waugh novel will be treated fairly.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the novelist's first name EVELYN and move its final N up two places, since in a down answer earlier letters are higher: EVENLY.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something fairly, without favouring either side, is doing it in a balanced, even-handed way.

clue.text: Tasty struggle on the field — good to hold back in fact

parts.note: a scrum is the rugby formation where the packs push against each other

indicators.note: holding something means keeping it inside, so one piece goes around another

parts.note: good in the moral, devout sense

indicators.note: the back of a word is its final letter, so only the last is kept

parts.note: the final letter of fact

explanation.surface: A rugby match praised as a tasty contest, where being good means holding back.
explanation.walkthrough: The rugby SCRUM comes first; PIOUS then holds the T that ends 'fact'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe food that is delicious and full of flavour; one is simply more colloquial.

clue.text: With sensitive information, European Community in bizarre protest

indicators.note: placing one thing in another puts it inside, so one piece sits within the other
something bizarre is strange and out of order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
EC is the standard abbreviation for the European Community

explanation.surface: A leaked dossier sparks an odd demonstration against the European Community.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Protest' looks like the subject of the sentence, but it is simply letters to rearrange; EC is the usual shorthand for the European Community.
explanation.definitionFit: A document classified at the highest level of security holds confidential material whose disclosure would cause harm.

clue.text: Anti-war protester curtailed agreement, one with weapon in hand?

indicators.note: to curtail is to cut short, so the final letter is removed

parts.note: a pact is a formal agreement
the Roman numeral for one
a clenched hand used for punching; the question mark flags the playful definition

explanation.surface: A peace campaigner breaks off a deal, ironically ending up armed.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that the peace campaigner is built partly from a punching hand; the question mark admits a hand is only loosely a weapon.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who opposes war and violence on principle and campaigns for peace is the standard meaning.

clue.text: After uprising, foolish to quit German city

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising means reading from the bottom upwards, so the order flips

parts.note: mad in the sense of crazy or foolish
to stop is to quit

explanation.surface: After a failed revolt, it would be foolish to leave a German city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uprising' suggests a revolt, but in a down clue it tells you to read MAD STOP from the bottom up.
explanation.definitionFit: Potsdam is the capital of Brandenburg, near Berlin, famous for its palaces and the 1945 conference.

clue.text: Family planning in the end sound as a bell?

parts.note: a clan is an extended family group

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, which is the only one kept

parts.note: the final letter of planning

explanation.surface: Is a family's careful planning ultimately sound as a bell?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound as a bell' is an idiom for being in perfect order, but here 'sound' is a verb: to ring as a bell does.
explanation.definitionFit: A loud metallic ringing noise is what a struck bell produces, so the verb fits exactly.

clue.text: Back hopper to lose tail

indicators.note: losing a tail means the last letter is dropped

parts.note: a frog is an animal that hops

explanation.surface: An animal that hops loses its tail, as tadpoles do on growing up.
explanation.walkthrough: Tadpoles really do lose their tails, which makes the surface neat. The definition comes from the phrase 'to and fro'.
explanation.definitionFit: In the phrase meaning forwards and backwards, the second word means away or in the reverse direction.

clue.text: Reshuffle by Tories: that's a serious state

indicators.note: a reshuffle moves things into new positions, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A Conservative cabinet reshuffle is described as a grave situation.
explanation.walkthrough: A reshuffle is a real political event, so the surface reads as news; here it simply rearranges the letters of 'by Tories'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sobriety means seriousness and solemnity of manner as well as not being drunk, so it is a grave condition.

clue.text: Serious about credit, it is ruined

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece surrounds another

parts.note: deep in the sense of profound or serious
CR is the accounting abbreviation for credit
taken as written

explanation.surface: A grave remark about someone's finances: their credit is ruined.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Serious' looks like the definition at the start, but the definition is at the end; CR for credit is standard accounting shorthand.
explanation.definitionFit: Something worn out, dilapidated and in very poor condition through age or neglect is described this way.

clue.text: Energy entering a crowd, a tiny shape-shifter

indicators.note: to enter something is to go inside it, so one piece is placed within another

parts.note: A plus MOB, a mob being a crowd
E is the symbol for energy in physics
the article taken as written, just before the definition

explanation.surface: A burst of energy runs through a crowd, turning up something tiny that keeps changing shape.
explanation.walkthrough: E goes inside A MOB, and a final A is added. The 'a' before 'tiny' serves the wordplay, not the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: This single-celled organism constantly changes form as it moves by pushing out pseudopods, so it is literally a microscopic shape-changer.

clue.text: Meat in fringes of fire, served lit

indicators.note: placing one thing in another puts it inside
fringes are the edges of something, so only the outer letters are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of fire
lamb is a kind of meat

explanation.surface: A chef brings meat to the table surrounded by flames and set alight.
explanation.walkthrough: LAMB sits inside the outer letters of fire. The whole surface describes the dish, which makes the clue neat.
explanation.definitionFit: A flambé dish has brandy or other spirit poured over it and ignited before it is brought to the table.

clue.text: Postprandial drink like coffee ultimately suits when knocked back

parts.note: to dig something is slang for to like it

indicators.note: ultimately means finally, so only the last letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter of coffee

indicators.note: knocking something back sends it backwards, so the letters are read in reverse

parts.note: to suit is to fit

explanation.surface: An after-dinner drink, like coffee, goes down well once it is knocked back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knocked back' sounds like drinking, fitting the surface, but it reverses FITS. 'Like' is the slang verb, not the comparison it seems.
explanation.definitionFit: Postprandial means after a meal; a digestif is a brandy or liqueur taken then to aid digestion.

clue.text: Went back for a moment

parts.note: informally, to split is to leave or go away
to back a proposal is to second it

explanation.surface: Someone returned briefly, just for a moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Went back' reads as one phrase meaning returned, but the words split apart: a slang verb for left, and a verb for support.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiny fraction of time, an instant, is the idiomatic sense of this phrase.

clue.text: I'm going to eat starters of real authenticity: Indian spices for dip

indicators.note: eating takes something inside, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: ta-ta is an informal British goodbye

indicators.note: starters are what come first, so only initial letters are kept

parts.note: the first letters of real and authenticity
masala is an Indian blend of ground spices

explanation.surface: A diner announces they will try some authentic Indian spices as a dip.
explanation.walkthrough: Ta-ta is an informal British goodbye, hence 'I'm going'. The Indian flavour is a false trail: the dip is Greek.
explanation.definitionFit: Taramasalata is a Greek spread of fish roe, eaten with bread or vegetables as a starter dip.

clue.text: In slayer, assume a possible offender?

indicators.note: putting something in another places it inside, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: a sword is a weapon that slays
to assume an expression or garment is to wear it

explanation.surface: A detective sizing up a killer as a likely suspect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Offender' suggests a criminal, but the offence meant is to polite ears; the question mark flags that. A sword is the slayer here, not a murderer.
explanation.definitionFit: An expletive or rude term causes offence to listeners, so it can be called something that offends.

clue.text: Great author has little time for criminal

parts.note: big means great in size
Kingsley or Martin Amis, English novelists
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A famous writer is too busy to bother with a lawbreaker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Great author' reads as one phrase, but it splits in two: an adjective, then the surname of Kingsley or Martin, both English novelists.
explanation.definitionFit: Marrying while already legally wed is an offence in many countries, so such a person is a lawbreaker.

clue.text: Beating ancient Greek volleyball team, perhaps, close to defeat

parts.note: a volleyball side has six players on court; 'perhaps' marks it as one example of a six
a citizen of Thebes, a city of ancient Greece, is 'of Thebes'

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only the final letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter of defeat

explanation.surface: A sports report: the ancient Greeks beat a volleyball team, coming close to losing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beating' looks like winning a match, but it is a noun for a punishment. Six of the best was a caning of six strokes in old British schools.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names a traditional school caning of six strokes, which is a physical thrashing.

clue.text: Arrangement of names, some without order, all together

indicators.note: an arrangement sets things out afresh, so the letters are shuffled into new positions

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: without means lacking, so letters are taken away from a word

parts.note: taken as written
the Order of Merit, a British honour, abbreviated OM

explanation.surface: A list of names, some out of order, is gathered in one place.
explanation.walkthrough: SOME loses OM to leave SE, which joins NAMES to be rearranged. 'Without order' looks like a description of a messy list.
explanation.definitionFit: This French phrase, borrowed into English, means in a body or as a group, everybody at once.

clue.text: Celebrate screening a show

indicators.note: a screen shields what is behind it, so one piece surrounds another

parts.note: to revel is to celebrate noisily
taken as written

explanation.surface: Throwing a party to mark the broadcast of a programme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Screening' and 'show' both suggest television, but screening hides A inside REVEL.
explanation.definitionFit: Both verbs mean to disclose or make something visible that was previously hidden.

clue.text: After better rock music for something spicy

parts.note: to cap something is to better or outdo it

indicators.note: to rock is to shake about, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Chasing a good rock concert with something hot to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rock music' reads as the genre, but 'rock' is the signal to jumble the next word. 'After' only places that jumble second.
explanation.definitionFit: Capsicum is the genus of peppers, including chillies, whose heat comes from capsaicin, so it is a hot pepper.

clue.text: Butterfly mark

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a butterfly with ragged wings and a white mark shaped like punctuation
second meaning: a punctuation sign marking a short pause

explanation.walkthrough: It looks like a mark on a butterfly's wing; in fact the insect's name and the punctuation sign are one word, the butterfly being named after its white mark.
explanation.definitionFit: The same word names a European orange butterfly species and the punctuation sign used to separate clauses.

clue.text: Grass-coated hide of elk smelt

indicators.note: a coat covers what is within, so one piece wraps around another

parts.note: a reed is a tall grass of wet places

indicators.note: a hide is an outer skin, so only the outside letters are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of elk

explanation.surface: A hunter notices an elk's hide, caked in grass, gives off a strong smell.
explanation.walkthrough: The outside of 'elk' sits within REED. 'Smelt' is the British past tense of smell, not the fish or the metalworking verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To stink or give off a strong unpleasant odour is the sense; both are past tense verbs.

clue.text: Wind is returning, low and menacing at first

indicators.note: returning means going back, so the letters are read backwards

parts.note: taken as written
to low is to moo, as cattle do

indicators.note: at first points to the beginning, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: the first letter of menacing

explanation.surface: A storm is coming back, the wind low and threatening from the start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Low' reads as quiet or near the ground, but it is the verb for a cow's call.
explanation.definitionFit: A simoom is a hot, dry, dust-laden desert wind of Arabia and North Africa.

clue.text: Lines often dedicated to defending harbours

indicators.note: to harbour is to shelter within, so the letters lie inside the words

parts.note: the letters run across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: Verses dedicated to the forces defending the nation's ports.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Harbours' looks like docks, fitting the defence theme, but it is the verb for holding something inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A lyric poem addressed to a person or thing is typically titled with that dedication, as in Keats's poem to a nightingale.

clue.text: Poorest off welcoming very brief stay

indicators.note: welcoming someone takes them in, so one piece goes inside another
something off has gone bad or wrong, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
V is the abbreviation for very

explanation.surface: The poorest are least well off yet still welcome a visitor staying only briefly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poorest off' suggests 'worst off', but 'off' tells you to rearrange POOREST, with V inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A short break in a journey, such as a night in a city between flights, is a short visit.

clue.text: Theatre boxes always the cheapest accommodation

indicators.note: to box something is to enclose it, so one piece surrounds another

parts.note: the stage stands for the theatre as a profession
e'er is the poetic contraction of ever, meaning always

explanation.surface: At the theatre, the boxes are always the cheapest seats.
explanation.walkthrough: Theatre boxes are usually the dearest seats, so the surface is a deliberate joke; 'boxes' is a verb here. E'er is the poetic form of ever.
explanation.definitionFit: On passenger ships, steerage was the lowest class of travel, below decks near the rudder.

clue.text: Daughter and curious man avoiding gentle breeze

indicators.note: to avoid something is to leave it out, so letters are removed

parts.note: D is the abbreviation for daughter
odd means strange or curious
taken as written
gent is short for gentleman

explanation.surface: A girl and an odd man steer clear of a light wind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gentle breeze' reads as one phrase, but 'gentle' is fodder: remove GENT to leave LE. Doddle is British slang for an easy task.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are informal for a task that is very easy, something done with no effort.
